new_statements.quote: Stress in UNT is phonemic and serves both to differentiate between words of different lexical classes and to mark person-aspectual distinctions on certain classes of verb. In general, stress is placed on the final syllable of words that end in a long vowel or a closed syllable, and (except in verbs) on the penultimate syllable of words ending in a short vowel. The stress on verbs is always on the final syllable, with the exception of verbs in the perfective aspect or in the second person, in which case the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The principal phonetic correlates of stress in UNT are increased duration and, to a lesser extent, amplitude of the syllabic nucleus

The quoted passage ('Stress in UNT is phonemic and serves both to differentiate.. The principal phonetic correlates of stress in UNT are increased duration and, to a lesser extent, amplitude of the syllabic nucleus') is there word for word. Surrounding text read: the section continues that stressed short vowels reach long-vowel duration, stressed long vowels get a rising contour, tone is phonemic only in cha:an 'ant' vs chaa:n 'ripe', and yes/no questions are marked by phrase-level…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge, final-syllable weight rule: stress the final syllable when the word ends in a long vowel or a closed syllable (heavy); when it ends in a short open vowel, stress the penult (non-verbs). Morphological overlay: verbs take final stress regardless of final-syllable weight, except perfective-aspect and 2nd-person forms, which take penultimate stress; stress is therefore 'phonemic' in that it distinguishes lexical classes and person/aspect. Confirmed independently by Beck 2008 (IJAL 74, p. 15: 'regularly assigned either to a final heavy syllable or to the penultimate syllable') and García-Vega & Tucker 2019 (JIPA, p. 59: 'predictable and regular notwithstanding a few exceptions'), the latter with acoustic evidence (duration, F0, vowel quality) from six Patla/Chicontla speakers.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in any source opened. Beck 2008 notes only that ideophones and reduplicated dynamic adverbs lack primary word-level stress (syllables given equal weight).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedge 'In general'; verbs final except perfective / 2nd person (penult); Beck 2008 adds 'stems affixed with final suffixes that obligatorily attract primary stress'; García-Vega & Tucker: 'a few exceptions (Beck 2011)'; ideophones and dynamic adverbs have no word-level stress; marginal phonemic tone in one word pair (cha:án 'ant' vs. chaá:n 'ripe') attributed to stress position within a long vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress (explicitly 'word-level' in Beck 2008); phrase-level prosody treated separately (rising intonation marks yes/no questions). García-Vega & Tucker measured target words inside a carrier phrase, not citation forms; Beck 2004 notes word-final devoicing/shortening of long vowels and laryngealization of final short vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: patl1234 'Patla-Chicontla Totonac' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for retired ISO [tot], split by change request 2006-085 (effective 2007-07-18) into Upper Necaxa Totonac [tku] = uppe1275 (Patla, Chicontla, San Pedro Tlalontongo, Cacahuatlán) and Tecpatlán Totonac [tcw] = tecp1235. Every source opened (Beck 2004, 2008; García-Vega & Tucker 2019; Puderbaugh 2019) describes Upper Necaxa Totonac from fieldwork in Patla and Chicontla, i.e. uppe1275; the statement should be keyed to uppe1275 (the earlier catalog ingest coded patl1234 not a distinct language with a duplicate of uppe1275 for exactly this reason). Nothing was found for Tecpatlán Totonac (tecp1235).

sources.note: Sec. 1.3 'Stress, tone, and prosody', printed p. 4 (p. 9): stress phonemic; final syllable if the word ends in a long vowel or closed syllable, otherwise (non-verbs) penult; verbs always final except perfective aspect / 2nd person (penult); correlates duration > amplitude, rising contour on stressed long vowels; phonemic tone in only one word pair; yes/no questions marked by phrase-level rising intonation. Sec. 2 (ideophones): no word-level stress.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.3 'Syllables and prosody', pp. 5-6, second-hand from Beck 2004/2008: 'Phonemic stress often distinguishes nouns from verbs.. In nouns, stress falls on the penultimate syllable, unless the word ends in a long vowel or a closed syllable, in which case the heavy weight draws stress to the final syllable. Verbs are always stress final, except suffixed verbs, which follow the same stress rules as nouns.' Notes cues to stress 'only sparsely documented'; her own H1-H2 models include stress as a factor.

sources.citation: Beck, David. 2008. Ideophones, adverbs, and predicate qualification in Upper Necaxa Totonac. International Journal of American Linguistics 74(1): 1-46. doi:10.1086/529462 (UAlberta Scholaris postprint, hdl 123456789/29466).
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Word-level stress', p. 15: 'In other word classes, stress is regularly assigned either to a final heavy syllable or to the penultimate syllable (the exceptions being V-final verb stems in most conjugations—which have final stress—and stems affixed with final suffixes that obligatorily attract primary stress), the phonetic correlate of stress being increased amplitude, vowel length, and (for long vowels) a marked pitch contour.' Ideophones and reduplicated dynamic adverbs lack primary word-level stress.
